subject: Population density, is a continuous or discrete variable?

messages.author: f6f8a0d70c721205
messages.subject: Population density, is a continuous or discrete variable?
parts:
hola,

Considering N as the number of animals, and S the area occupied or the study area, it is common to express the density as D = N / S.

D often expressed as decimal, eg 3.3 deer/km2.

This is numerically clear, but biologically is 3 or 4 deer/km2.

If N can be explained by a Poisson distribution, also D?

or we must to use a distinct distribution, eg Gamma?

muchas gracias, saludos

Salvador Mandujano

messages.author: 527d9b3ec7deff2d
messages.subject: Re: Population density, is a continuous or discrete variable?
parts:
Hi Salvador,

Density is the count of objects per unit of space, similar to how a rate is often the count of events per unit of time.  In both cases, the count is the quantity of interest and is arguably best described as a discrete random variable.  You can often model densities and rates as continuous variables without a problem in a number of circumstances, but sometimes the error structure will be poorly approximated.  Treating N as a Poisson random variable with log(area) as an offset essentially gives you a model of density.

messages.author: 2840cf87ab6c68e9
messages.subject: Re: Population density, is a continuous or discrete variable?
parts:
Salvador,

To piggyback off of Daniel's great response, I will answer the other part of your question.

I understand any misgivings you may have with stating 3.3 deer/km2. This density estimate suggests that there are 3 individuals plus another 1/3 of an individual per km2 (that poor 1/3 of a deer is in trouble). As you mentioned, this doesn't make sense biologically but it is common to report density estimates this way.

To be more biologically realistic, you could change the way you report density into unit area per whole individual. Simply divide your current density estimate by 1 and you will swap the units around. Taking your example of 3.3 deer/km2, we can convert it to:

1/3.3 = 1 deer per 0.303 km2

It can be changed back by:

1/0.303 = 3.3 deer per km2

Hopefully this helps.

Best,
DMW

messages.author: 0216939e087e502c
messages.subject: RE: Population density, is a continuous or discrete variable?
parts:
Hola Salvador,

here's my attempt at a reply.

You are wondering about the difference between a discrete random variable and the expected value of the discrete random variable. The random variable is discrete (there are N = 0, 1,2,3, 4, .... real deer in some area). However, we characterize that random variable by a number which (in the case of a Poisson) is the expected value, which you can imagine as the average if we could replicate the same "situation" a million times. This average is continuous. Getting 3.3 deer then means that we seem to be a little more certain that it's 3 rather than 4 deer in the area. So even though the random variable is discrete, our characterization of it in the statistical model is continuous.

This is not unique to biology and is also what happens all the time when we take averages. For instance, in school in Switzerland we had discrete marks (e.g., 1, 1.5, ... 5.5 and 6) for tests we took and in the end of the year these were averaged to something like, say, 4.8. So the average "behaviour" of each pupil was characterized by a number which was typically impossible to achieve, because the actual marks were discrete in half-integer steps.

The world is full with discrete random variables which we characterize by a continuous average, whether in a formal statistical model or just in more colloquial usage. So we just have to get used to that I guess.

Best regards  --  Marc

messages.author: 00ebeb6e0521112d
messages.subject: RE: Population density, is a continuous or discrete variable?
parts:
And one more: we're typically a little vague in our language about what we mean by "density". Look at the algebra. In a typical model for "density" we have something like this for the number of animals N inhabiting a site:

N ~ Poisson(lambda)

So, the realized "density", or population size, is N. This is a discrete random variable of course (because there are no third-deer). However, in the model, we characterize N by its expected value, which is lambda, and this is also called density, but it's the expected density.

So, in this sense, you can claim that "density" can be both discrete and continuous, but you must know which meaning of density you're talking about: the realized or the expected.

Best regards  --  Marc

hola DMW

I appreciate your comments.

That's right, for ranchers customary to refer to the number of hectares per animal unit. In fact, some wildlife managers in Mexico prefer to report data such as 1 deer per 30 hectares. Ranchers call it as "index pasture" (I do not know if English has the same meaning… “índice de agostadero” en español).

But among biologists it is common to report the density in terms of average individuals by surface (3.3 deer / km2).

I think it is simply a different numerical approach.

saludos

Salvador

messages.author: 4a635fe980c8c1cd
messages.subject: Re: Population density, is a continuous or discrete variable?
parts:
Hi Salvador,

The beauty of the models discussed in Royle & Dorazio 2008, Kery and Schaub 2012, and Kery and Royle 2016 is that variance in the state parameter can modeled directly within the estimation process rather than after the fact.  E.g., a call in unmarked, let's say fm <- multinomPois(~suitability ~1, umf), is estimating abundance accounting for imperfect detection while simultaneously estimating the log-linear abundance effect of suitability.  

In most (if not nearly all) applications, density/abundance is modeled using a log-link function, because the number of activity centers (in a spatial capture-recapture model, say) or the number of birds (in a distance model, say) is a non-negative discrete random variable within a defined space (a pixel or ||S|| in scr, or the truncated radius area in a distance model), and the log-link suitably constrains the outcome.  Realized density is generally derived as N/area of prescribed space.  Distance and SCR models explicitly define space, which allows direct density inference, and models that do not explicitly define space generally do not, but the estimation process is extremely similar (#things at a site w/ size x, vs #things at a site with unknown size).  However, the functional shape of an expected density effect could be modeled in any number of ways, which may be something that deserves attention in applied practice.  As the book describes, abundance could be modeled using a spline, etc.

Once density or abundance has been estimated, both realized and expected estimates are available.  N[i] is the estimate of realized abundance (in a known space or not), lambda[i] is the estimate of expected abundance (in a known space or not) within a Bugs-language model; the ranef estimates in unmarked relate to realized estimates (vs. expected estimates derived from predict).

Cheers,

John

messages.author: 00ebeb6e0521112d
messages.subject: AW: Population density, is a continuous or discrete variable?
parts:
Dear Salvador,

 

You find Winbugs a nightmare ? Well, then you haven’t met cases where it is virtually impossible to find starting values that work for JAGS ;)

 

I am not sure about your question below. In hierarchical distance sampling, you embed an abundance model (for the number of individuals per site, N_i) into a model that describes the distance sampling observation model (e.g., a multinomial if you bin the distances). So, as an integral part of the model, you have an expression like this:

 

N_i ~ Poisson(lambda_i)

 

Then, you can naturally model spatial (or temporal, or spatiotemporal) variation in density exactly like in any old Poisson regression, that is, as in a Poisson GLM with log link function. That is, you write the log of the expected density as a linear of other function of covariates.

 

log(lambda_i) = alpha + beta * X_i ........

 

The beauty of such hierarchical models is that you are now back the same old GLM that most of us have been using forever and hence you can do all you do with GLMs inside of this hierarchical model. Of course, this includes extensions such as wiggly relationships as in GAMS or additional random effects as in spatial models.

 

Best regards  --- Marc
